In the Guided Projects you learned one part of the grammar of graphics at a time, on
both of your datasets. In this Challenge Project you choose and combine those tools to
answer **two or three questions of your own** about **one dataset**, your Sports
Data, and you publish a **report** and **slides** that tell
what you found. You'll present one of your two Challenge Projects on Friday, December 4.

**AI use: Level 2 (AI Collaboration).** See "AI use" in **Reference**.
**Due:** see Blackboard for the due date and time.

## Learning outcomes

This project assesses the course learning outcomes (syllabus). You will:

- Assess the accuracy and honesty of data visualizations by applying principles of
  graphical integrity.
- Design original data graphics that maximize data density and minimize chartjunk,
  using principles such as data-ink maximization and multifunctional graphical
  elements.
- Analyze how visual design choices (e.g., scale, proportion, labeling, and layout)
  influence the interpretation of quantitative information.
- Identify and define the core components of the grammar of graphics, including data,
  aesthetics, geoms, stats, scales, coordinates, and facets.
- Construct visualizations using layered grammar and describe the role of each
  component while building a plot.
- Apply appropriate geoms and aesthetics from the grammar of graphics to explore
  relationships in a dataset.
- Compare and contrast different visualizations (obtained with the grammar of
  graphics) to evaluate how changes in aesthetics, geoms, or scales affect the
  interpretation of data.
- Design and implement custom visualizations using the grammar of graphics,
  incorporating advanced features such as faceting, themes, and coordinate
  transformations to effectively communicate insights from data.

## Get ready (once, about 10 minutes)

All of this happens in your **`cis-3901-projects`** project in Posit Cloud.

**1. Your data file.** This project reads **`data/sports.csv`**, the same file as
GP13. Don't change or overwrite it: your script builds everything it needs from it.

**2. Add the starter files.** Download **`cp_sports_starter.zip`** from the
Blackboard assignment. In `cis-3901-projects`, go to the **top folder** (`project`) →
**Upload** → the zip. It adds three files:

```default
scripts/cp_sports.R                     the code: data moves and every figure
reports/cp_sports_report.qmd            your report: questions, findings, audit
presentations/cp_sports_slides.qmd      your slides: your talk
```

These are the **only** files of this project. Your site also has
`sports_report.qmd` and `sports_slides.qmd` from October: they aren't used here,
so leave them alone.

**3. Run Section 0** of `scripts/cp_sports.R`. It checks your data file and prints a
summary of your columns (never rows), as in GP13.

**4. Render both files, commit and push.** Both render from day one ("Not done
yet." where a figure isn't made yet). Open both links:

- `https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/cis-3901-projects/reports/cp_sports_report.html`
- `https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/cis-3901-projects/presentations/cp_sports_slides.html`

**Your Guided Project work is your starting point, not your project.** You may copy
and revise figure code from `scripts/gp13_scales_facets.R` (or GP11–GP12). A project
made only of Guided Project plots isn't complete: your figures must answer **your**
questions.

**Tidy as needed.** ggplot2 needs tidy data, so tidy anything your questions need (the
Module 10 operations apply). Tidying itself isn't graded in this project.

## Do the project in six tasks

Each task: the code goes in the **script**, your words go in the **report** (and the
slides). Render and push whenever you stop. Unlike the Guided Projects, the script has
no PASS / TO DO checks for each task: the checklist in **Finish and submit** is your
check.

### Task 1 · Your questions {#task-1}

**Goal:** Two or three questions of your own that tell one story.

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| Questions | Write two or three questions, one sentence each, naming the **outcome** and the **groups compared**. They connect: for example, an overall pattern, then who it differs for, then whether it holds over time or within subgroups | Your instructor approves them in the proposal; the final must match or explain changes |
| Report | Put your questions at the top of the report and on your **Question** slide | Your instructor reads them (counts under Questions and data) |

Two questions make a complete, full-credit project. More questions or more slides
don't earn more credit.

**Example (penguins, not your data):**

| # | Question | Outcome | Groups compared |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Do the three penguin species differ in body mass? | body mass (g) | species |
| 2 | Does the species difference hold for both sexes? | body mass (g) | species × sex |

**Question patterns that work:** a rate within groups (who has the outcome more
often?); an overall pattern, then a subgroup; before and after a season, a rule change
or a year ("compared to what?", I6); the same comparison in panels.

#### Your project is yours

Several of you work with the same dataset. That's fine, but your Challenge Project must
be **your own and substantially different** from every other student's, including
classmates who use the same data.

- **Your questions are independent.** No question may match another student's: the
  same outcome compared across the same groups counts as a match, even if it's worded
  differently.
- **Your figures and writing are your own.** You may talk about ideas with classmates.
  Write your own code, make your own figures, and write your own findings, limits and
  "why it matters."
- **Say where help came from.** If a classmate, a tutor or an AI tool shaped your
  work, say so: in your AI log for AI tools, and in a one-line acknowledgment in your
  report for people.
- **Be ready to explain it.** You should be able to explain any figure or line of code
  in your project, on December 4 or if I ask before then.

Projects that are copies of each other (same questions, same figures) don't meet this
requirement, and copying falls under the Catawba College Honor Code.

### Task 2 · Prepare your data for your questions {#task-2}

**Goal:** Make the groups, years or subsets your questions need, and show what each
step did.

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| Script | One section per data move: `mutate()` a year or a group, `filter()`, or lumping groups with care. Print the rows and the groups (with n) **before and after** each move | Your instructor reads the code and output (counts under Questions and data) |
| Report | For each move, one line: what it does and why your question needs it. In your **Data** paragraph and slide: where the data come from, what one row is, how many rows, and what you made or filtered | Your instructor reads it |

Never drop or combine a group silently: say what you removed or lumped, and how many
rows that was.

**Example:**

| Move | Code | Why my question needs it | Before → after |
|---|---|---|---|
| Drop penguins with no sex recorded | `filter(!is.na(sex))` | Question 2 compares sexes | 344 → 333 rows (11 removed; said in the report) |
| Make a period (gapminder) | `mutate(period = if_else(year < 1980, "before 1980", "1980 on"))` | A before-and-after comparison | 1,704 rows; 12 years → 2 periods, 852 rows each |

### Task 3 · Figures that answer your questions {#task-3}

**Goal:** At least one figure for each question, each one making its finding easy to
see.

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| Script | Make each figure in its own chunk (`## ---- fig1 ----`, `fig2`, …). Across the project: **at least one figure with facets**, and **at least one with a deliberate scale or coordinate choice** (log or percent scale, zoom with `coord_cartesian()`, flipped axes) | Your instructor reads the code and figures (counts under Figures and grammar of graphics choices) |
| Report | Under each figure: a **headline** that states the finding; a **grammar line** (below); one or two sentences on what the figure shows | Your instructor reads it |

For every figure:

- **Headline states the finding** (P2): "Gentoo penguins are the heaviest species",
  not "Body mass by species".
- **Grammar line:** name the figure's components and their roles. Example: "data: one
  row per penguin; aesthetics: species → x, body mass → y, sex → panels; geom: points
  with a mean marker; scale: y in grams, fixed across panels; facet: sex."
- **Alt text** (`fig-alt`): one sentence that says what the reader should see.
- **n for every group**, in labels, strips or the subtitle.
- **Colors:** run `color_check()` (at least 20 in all three rows), and color is never
  the only cue (D4).
- **Comparing groups:** show each group's n, and use **rates within groups** rather
  than counts where the groups differ in size (I4). If a group is small, keep it
  visible and say so; don't drop or lump it without saying why.
- **No private person's name** in any figure, table or slide (Boston Marathon names,
  bibs and teams; powerlifters' names; MMA judges).

### Task 4 · Integrity audit {#task-4}

**Goal:** Check every final figure against the Module 14 codes, and show one
improvement.

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| Report | A table, one row per final figure: the **codes it meets** (at least two), **one fix you made**, and **why** | Your instructor reads it (counts under Integrity and data-ink) |
| Before and after | For **at least one** figure, show the earlier version beside the final one (your GP13 version counts), with one sentence on how the change alters what a reader sees | Your instructor reads it |

**Example:**

| Figure | Codes it meets | One fix I made | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Life expectancy by continent, 1952–2007 (gapminder) | I2, D3 | Labeled the lines directly and removed the legend | Readers had to match five colors to a legend, and color was the only cue (D4) |

The 14 codes are in **Reference**.

### Task 5 · Choose your path {#task-5}

**Goal:** Go further in one of two ways. Both earn the same credit: what counts is how
well your figures answer your questions, not which path you take.

**Path A · Go deeper with the tools you know.** Combine what you learned in GP11–GP13
more ambitiously than any single Guided Project task did. For example:

- **layer** stats, scales and facets in one figure (rates with error bars, in panels,
  on a percent axis);
- **show uncertainty** for every group comparison (error bars or resampled clouds);
- **annotate** important events or values on the figure (I2);
- **order** groups so the finding reads first;
- **replace** several separate plots with one set of small multiples that share an
  axis.

**Path B · Bring in one new R tool.** Learn one package on your own and use it for at
least one figure. Your skills carry over: most tools still map data to aesthetics,
draw geoms and use scales. Examples: `patchwork` (combine figures into one layout),
`ggrepel` (direct labels that don't overlap), `ggridges` (distributions for many
groups), `plotly` or `ggiraph` (interactive figures on your report page).

If you choose Path B:

- **Explain the mapping:** add a short section to your report, "How my new tool fits
  the grammar of graphics": which aesthetics, geoms, stats, scales or facets it uses or
  replaces.
- **Keep the course rules:** `%>%`, `color_check()` passes, color is never the only
  cue, alt text on every figure.
- **It must work where your project lives:** it installs in Posit Cloud, and your
  report and slides still render and publish.
- **Cite it** in your Sources, and log any AI help with it.
- **If it doesn't work by the deadline,** go back to Path A for that figure and say so
  in one line. That isn't a penalty.

Say in your proposal which path you'll take (and for Path B, which tool and which
figure).

### Task 6 · Tell the story {#task-6}

**Goal:** A report and slides that a reader can follow from question to "why it
matters."

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| Report | The story arc (P1): **question, data, finding, limits, why it matters**. Differences, not causes. Small groups named, with their n | Your instructor reads it (counts under Story and interpretation) |
| Changes | One line for each change from your approved proposal, and why | Your instructor compares it with your proposal |
| Slides | See **Build your slides** below | Your instructor reads them |

**Example (penguins):**

| Stage | Example |
|---|---|
| Question | Do the three species differ in body mass, and does the difference hold for both sexes? |
| Data | Palmer penguins: one row is one penguin; 344 rows, 333 with sex recorded |
| Finding | Gentoo penguins are the heaviest species, for females and for males |
| Limits | Three islands and three seasons; differences, not causes |
| Why it matters | Comparing the species without splitting by sex could hide where the gap is largest |

## Build your slides

**Goal:** A short talk that a listener can follow, about 7 minutes long.

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| Slides | Open `presentations/cp_sports_slides.qmd`. Replace each prompt with your own words. A figure appears by naming its chunk from the script. Render | Your instructor reads them (counts under Story and interpretation); if you present this project, your talk uses this deck |

- [ ] **Title** (in the YAML): what is this about, and who made it?
- [ ] **Question(s):** your investigative questions.
- [ ] **Data:** where it's from, what one row is, how many rows, what you made or
  filtered.
- [ ] **One slide per finding:** a headline that states the finding, then the figure.
- [ ] **What it shows, and its limits:** differences, not causes; small groups; what
  the data can't tell us.
- [ ] **Why it matters:** one or two sentences on what your findings mean for the
  audience.
- [ ] **Sources and AI use:** the data citation, any new tool, one line on AI use.

About **5–7 slides that show a finding** (about one minute each), plus the title,
question, data and closing slides. No code on the slides. **Speaker notes are public**
on the web: leave them out. Every figure has `fig-alt`.

::: {.callout-important}
## Edit the code in the script. The report and the slides only read it.

Your words live in the report and the slides.
:::

### The 14 codes (Module 14)

**Integrity:** I1 Size matches the numbers (Lie Factor) · I2 Label clearly; annotate
important events · I3 Show data variation, not design variation · I4 Standardized units
(rates, per capita) · I5 No more dimensions than the data · I6 Compared to what?

**Data-ink:** D1 Always plot the data · D2 Mute the grid; data ink first · D3 Label
directly, not only through a legend · D4 Color is never the only cue

**Presenting:** P1 Story arc: question, data, finding, limits, why it matters · P2 The
headline states the finding · P3 One message per slide · P4 Explain a figure aloud:
axes, where to look, what it means

### Privacy

Your data file may stay as you downloaded it from SCORE, names included. Your report
and slides never show a private person's name: never use a name, bib, team or judge
column (Boston Marathon, powerlifting, MMA) in a figure, table or slide. Professional
athletes and teams are public figures.

### Grading (percentage ranges in the rubric)

**Levels (all criteria):** Exemplary 90–100% · Proficient 80–89% · Developing 65–79% ·
Beginning 1–64% · No Response 0%.

| Criterion | Weight | Looks at |
|---|---|---|
| Questions and data | 15% | Two or three independent questions naming outcome and groups; data moves with why and n before and after; matches your approved proposal, or changes explained |
| Figures and grammar of graphics choices | 25% | Each question answered by a figure; components chosen for a reason; grammar lines; facets and a scale or coordinate choice; Path A depth or Path B mapping |
| Integrity and data-ink | 20% | Integrity audit with one before-and-after; group comparisons with n and rates; color check, never color alone; specific alt text; no private names |
| Story and interpretation | 20% | Question, data, finding, limits, why it matters; headlines state findings; differences, not causes; small groups named; slides that show findings |
| Code and publishing | 10% | One script feeds the report and the slides; both render and are published; no template text left |
| AI disclosure | 10% | AI use line in your report and slides, AI log typed in Blackboard (or the no-AI statement), attestation, and copies of all AI conversations uploaded |

An idea of your own that helps the reader see the finding (an angle, a comparison, an
order, an annotation) is what separates Exemplary from Proficient. Decoration doesn't
count; an idea that distorts the data or breaks the color rules earns no credit.

### Oral presentation (Friday, December 4)

You present **one** of your two Challenge Projects (chosen in your proposal) from the
slides you submitted. About **10 minutes each:** 7 minutes to talk, 2 minutes for questions,
1 minute to change over. Rehearse with a timer; if you're over, cut a slide rather than speak
faster. In the last class you give a 1–2 minute preview: your question and one figure
explained aloud.

| Criterion | Weight | Looks at |
|---|---|---|
| Investigative questions and data | 25% | States the questions, naming outcome and groups; what the data are, what one row is, how many rows |
| Findings and figures | 25% | Each headline states the finding; each figure explained aloud (axes, where to look, what it means); differences, not causes; small groups with n |
| Limits and why it matters | 25% | What the data can't tell us; what the findings mean for the audience |
| Delivery, timing and questions | 25% | Within 7 minutes; audible and paced; one message per slide; answers questions clearly and explains your own choices |

Same levels as above.
